etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English pouren (“to pour”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Northern French purer (“to sift (grain), pour out (water)”), from Latin pūrō (“to purify”), from pūrus (“pure”). Compare Middle Dutch afpuren (“to pour off, drain”).

To pour displaced several Middle English verbs:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause (liquid, or liquid-like substance) to flow in a stream, either out of a container or into it.
(transitive, figurative) To send out as in a stream or a flood; to cause (an emotion) to come out; to cause to escape.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, prologue]:
quote.text: How London doth pour out her citizens.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Samuel 1:15:
quote.text: […]  I haue drunke neither wine nor strong drinke, but haue powred out my soule before the Lord.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ezekiel 7:8:
quote.text: Now will I shortly powre out my furie vpon thee, and accomplish mine anger vpon thee […]

quote.citation: 1637, John Milton, A Mask presented at Ludlow Castle, 1634, lines 710-711:
quote.text: Wherefore did Nature pour her bounties forth / With such a full and unwithdrawing hand?

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, “Can China clean up fast enough?”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: At the same time, it is pouring money into cleaning up the country.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To send forth from, as in a stream; to discharge uninterruptedly.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], (please specify |epistle=I to IV), London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Is it for thee the linnet pours his throat?

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To flow, pass, or issue in a stream; to fall continuously and abundantly.

quote.citation: 2014 October 27, Taylor Swift, Imogen Heap, “Clean (Taylor's Version)”, in 1989 (Taylor's Version)‎[1], performed by Taylor Swift, published 2023 October 27:
quote.text: The rain came pouring downWhen I was drownin', that's when I could finally breathe

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Of a beverage, to be on tap or otherwise available for serving to customers.
(intransitive) To move in a throng, as a crowd.

quote.citation: 1716, John Gay, Trivia: Or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London:
quote.text: In the rude throng pour on with furious pace.

quote.citation: 1964 June 16, “All Eyes On Lema At U.S. Open This Week”, in The Indianapolis Star, volume 62, number 11, Indianapolis, Ind., page 22:
quote.text: The bluebloods of golf began pouring into the sweltering nation’s capital yesterday for the 64th U.S. Open championship, and the hottest topic was not Arnold Palmer or Jack Nicklaus, but Champagne Tony Lema.

quote.citation: 2011 January 8, Chris Bevan, “Arsenal 1-1 Leeds”, in BBC:
quote.text: In a breathless finish Arsenal poured forward looking for a winner but Leeds held out for a deserved replay after Bendtner wastefully fired wide and Schmeichel acrobatically kept out Denilson's rasping effort

quote.citation: 2003, John Brian Newman, B. S. Choo, Advanced concrete technology: Volume 2:
quote.text: Over this time period, the first concrete pour has not only lost workability but has started to set so that it is no longer affected by the action of a vibrator.

quote.citation: 2023 June 14, “Network News: Concrete for Old Oak Common - and consent for Curzon Street viaduct”, in RAIL, number 985, page 22:
quote.text: HS2 Ltd has completed the first base-slab concrete pour at the western end of Old Oak Common station.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) A downpour; a flood of precipitation.

quote.citation: 1831, Susan Ferrier, Destiny; or, the Chief's Daughter‎[2], page 84:
quote.text: Then, as if to give the lie to the offensive insinuation, he mounted his horse, and rode home ten miles in a pour of rain, without a great coat or umbrella.

quote.citation: 1953, Samuel Beckett, Watt, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Grove Press, published 1959, →OCLC:
quote.text: But then one of Mr. Knott's men would have had to put on his coat and hat and turn out, as likely as not in the pitch dark, and in torrents of rain in all probability, and grope his way in the dark in the pours of rain, with the pot of food in his hand, a wretched and ridiculous figure, to where the dog lay.
